Hi, I am trying to fit a state space model using Nimble.

But, I am not sure what is wrong. I followed the steps shown in this example https://nature.berkeley.edu/~pdevalpine/nimbleExamples/particle_filter/pfExample.html

Here is the model. T1 and T2 are latent states. Te, Ti, and q are observed data. deltaT is constant. C1, C2, R1, R2, and R3 are parameters.  sigma1,2,3 are gaussian noise with mean 0.

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-lfxpJ8mGnGQ/WiCo8YvDxII/AAAAAAAAMDE/Q56g2o4v-58mmE-4nNgHIpBn550xcwD3wCLcBGAs/s1600/456.png>

I recovered my code and data below. In the example, we didn't initialize x (latent state). And there is one state. But, my case, I got errors if I didn';t initialize it. Also, I have two states (T1 and T2).

I tried to put T1 and T2 together in a matrix, but it didn't work.

Can you give  me any suggestions?

Thank you so much..!!

library(nimble)

rm(list=ls())

X <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ecosang/tt/master/bldg1_dat.csv", sep=";", header=FALSE)

## Set the names of the columns in X

names(X) <- c("t","Te","Ti","q")

set.seed(1)

dim(X$Te)

## define the model

stateSpaceCode <- nimbleCode({

  C1 ~ T(dnorm(100, 5),90,100)

  C2 ~ T(dnorm(50, 5),40,50)

  R1 ~ T(dnorm(1, 0.5),0.001,2)

  R2 ~ T(dnorm(2, 1),0.001,4)

  R3 ~ T(dnorm(0.5, 0.25),0.001,1)

  sigma1~dunif(1e-03,2)

  sigma2~dunif(1e-03,2)

  sigma3~dunif(1e-03,2)

  T1[1] ~ dnorm(8,sigma1)

  T2[1] ~ dnorm(12,sigma2)

  for (t in 1:(TT-1)){

    T1[t+1]~dnorm(mean=( T1[t]+((T2[t]-T1[t])/(C1*R2)+(Te[t]-T1[t])/(C1*R1))*dt  ),sd=sigma1)

    T2[t+1]~dnorm(mean=( T2[t]+((Ti[t]-T2[t])/(C2*R3)+(T1[t]-T2[t])/(C2*R2))*dt  ),sd=sigma2)

    q[t]~dnorm(mean=(Ti[t]-T2[t])/R3,sd=sigma3)

  }

  q[TT]~dnorm(mean=(Ti[TT]-T2[TT])/R3,sd=sigma3)

})

## define data, constants, and initial values

dat <- list(q=X$q,Ti=X$Ti,Te=X$Te[-length(X$Te)]) #X$Te

constants <- list(

    dt = 1,

    TT=(dim(X)[1])

)

inits <- list(

  C1=100,

  C2=50,

  R1=1,

  R2=2,

  R3=0.5,

  sigma1=0.5,

  sigma2=0.5,

  sigma3=0.5,

  T1=rep(8,(dim(X)[1])),

  T2=rep(12,(dim(X)[1]))

)

## build the model

stateSpaceModel <- nimbleModel(stateSpaceCode,

                              data = dat,

                              constants = constants,

                              init=inits,

                              check = FALSE)

## create MCMC specification for the state space model

stateSpaceMCMCconf <- configureMCMC(stateSpaceModel, nodes = NULL)

## add a block pMCMC sampler for a, b, sigPN, and sigOE

stateSpaceMCMCconf$addSampler(target = c('C1', 'C2','R1', 'R2','R3', 'sigma1', 'sigma2', 'sigma3'),

                              type = 'RW_PF_block', control = list(latents = c('T1','T2')))

stateSpaceMCMC <- buildMCMC(stateSpaceMCMCconf)

compiledList <- compileNimble(stateSpaceModel, stateSpaceMCMC, resetFunctions = TRUE)

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for asking and for including an example of your error!  One current limitation of NIMBLE's particle filtering methods (as I think you realized) is that all of the latent states have to be held in the same variable.  This should be fixed in  a future version of NIMBLE, but for now you will have to model your two latent state variables (T1 and T2) as a single matrix.  I rewrote your model slightly to accomplish this, turning T1 and T2 into a single matrix T_12, where T_12[1, t] corresponds to T1[t] and T_12[2, t] corresponds to T2[t].

stateSpaceCode <- nimbleCode({

  C1 ~ T(dnorm(100, 5),90,100)

  C2 ~ T(dnorm(50, 5),40,50)

  R1 ~ T(dnorm(1, 0.5),0.001,2)

  R2 ~ T(dnorm(2, 1),0.001,4)

  R3 ~ T(dnorm(0.5, 0.25),0.001,1)

  sigma1~dunif(1e-03,2)

  sigma2~dunif(1e-03,2)

  sigma3~dunif(1e-03,2)

  T_12[1, 1] ~ dnorm(8,sigma1)

  T_12[2, 1] ~ dnorm(12,sigma2)

  for (t in 1:(TT-1)){

    T_12[1, t+1]~dnorm(mean=( T_12[1, t]+((T_12[2, t]-T_12[1, t])/(C1*R2)+(Te[t]-T_12[1, t])/(C1*R1))*dt  ),sd=sigma1)

    T_12[2, t+1]~dnorm(mean=( T_12[2, t]+((Ti[t]-T_12[2, t])/(C2*R3)+(T_12[1, t]-T_12[2, t])/(C2*R2))*dt  ),sd=sigma2)

    q[t]~dnorm(mean=(Ti[t]-T_12[2, t])/R3,sd=sigma3)

  }

  q[TT]~dnorm(mean=(Ti[TT]-T_12[2, TT])/R3,sd=sigma3)

})

I also changed the initial values, so that T_12 was given a matrix of initial values, and updated the "latents" control list argument for the "RW_PF_block" sampler to be "T_12" instead of "c(T1, T2)".  After this, the particle MCMC algorithm was able to compile and run successfully.  Let me know if you try this out and it doesn't work though, or if you have any other questions.  Thanks again!

Hello,

We are having a similar problem to the one described by Lu Zhang with the implementation of a spatial hierarchical model using NIMBLE. A minimal reproducible example including data to run the model is attached as the file "minimal_example_KCNK.R".

We have written a two-level hierarchical model with four hyperparameters: alpha, sigma, tau and lambda as follows:

# define hierarchical model with BUGS code
siteHierarchyCode <- nimble::nimbleCode({

  # ---
  # Define priors for hyperparameters
  # ---

  # mean of means
  alpha ~ dnorm(mean = 0,sd = 1000)

  # sd of means : approximates Jeffrey's prior (inverse prior)
  tau ~ dgamma(shape = 0.0001, rate = 0.0001)

  # sd at each site : approximates Jeffrey's prior (inverse prior)
  sigma ~ dgamma(shape = 0.0001, rate = 0.0001)

  # correlation length at each site : approximates Jeffrey's prior (inverse prior)
  lambda ~ dgamma(shape = 0.0001, rate = 0.0001)

  # ---
  # Define hierarchical model at each site
  # ---

  for (i in 1:I){ # for each site

    # the mean is drawn from a univariate gaussian distribution
    mu[i] ~ dnorm(mean = alpha,sd = tau) # distribution of mean at site i
    mat_mu_i[i,1:J_i[i]] <- mu[i] * mat_ones[i,1:J_i[i]]

    # the covariance matrix is defined by an exponential variogram function
    Sigma[1:J_i[i],1:J_i[i],i] <-  sigma^2 * (1 - exp( -(d_ij[1:J_i[i],
                                                              1:J_i[i],
                                                              i]/lambda) ))

    # observations are multivariate normal
    y[i,1:J_i[i]] ~ dmnorm(mat_mu_i[i,1:J_i[i]],
                           cov = Sigma[1:J_i[i],1:J_i[i],i])

  }

})

We run the model using the following code:
#'
#' # Create NIMBLE model and run #
#'

# actually create the model
siteModel <-
  nimble::nimbleModel(code = siteHierarchyCode,
                      constants = siteConst,
                      data = siteData,
                      inits = siteInit,
                      name = 'siteModel')

# compile the model
CsiteModel <- nimble::compileNimble(siteModel)

# create compile and run MCMC
siteModelConf <- nimble::configureMCMC(model = siteModel,
                                       print=T,
                                       multivariateNodesAsScalars=T)

siteModelConf$addMonitors(c('alpha','tau','sigma','lambda'))

siteModelMCMC <-
  nimble::buildMCMC(siteModelConf)
CsiteModelMCMC <-
  nimble::compileNimble(siteModelMCMC, project = siteModel)

CsiteModelMCMC$run(10^5)

While the model complies and runs, the hyperparameters lambda and sigma remain at their initial values, while hyperparameters alpha and tau appear to have been sampled by the MCMC. We have tried modifying the initial values and have so far had no success.

We would like to know, is this problem due to the way the model is defined, or, is there a specific method for running this model such that lambda and sigma are computed?

Thank you,

Karina Cucchi and Nura Kawa
Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, U.C. Berkeley

I built your model and checked on which parts are validly initialized from your siteInit and resulting calculations or not. Were you maybe exploring different model formulations and really want sigma^2 * exp(-d_ij[....] / lambda), which would put sigma^2 on the diagonal?

Perry

messages.body_plain:
Dear Yan,

There are three ways you could consider using or translating such functions.

1. You could translate them into nimbleFunctions.  Obviously that provides limited features but can work well for primarily numerical functions.

2. You could translate them to C/C++/Fortran and call them from nimbleFunctions as an externalCall (see help(nimbleExternalCall)).

3. You could call them from nimbleFunctions an R calls, which are executed in R, even from compiled nimbleFunctions.  Often a wrapper will be needed to achieve clean types.  Although this can impose some performance cost due to R execution, it is the fastest way to make them work.  See help(nimbleRcall).

Regarding posterior predictive p-values, we are under way implementing the calibrated ppp method of Hjort et al. (JASA 2006, DOI 10.1198/016214505000001393).  Let us know if that is what you are looking for.

Perry

I am trying to fit this SCR model with discrete space in nimble, and I am getting an error message: Error in envRefInferField(x, what, getClass(class(x)), selfEnv) :‘Sgrid’ is not a valid field or method name for reference class “code_MID_2_modelClass_UID_17_UID_18”

I am having issues trying to define the state space using xy coordinates of all cells of a grid (matrix Sgrid), instead of x and y limits - my state space area is irregular, and will also have an habitat covariate (forest type) associated with each grid cell.

Here is the code:

code <- nimbleCode({

    lam0 ~ dunif(0,5)
    sigma ~ dunif(0,5)
    psi ~ dunif(0,1)

    for(i in 1:M) {
       z[i] ~ dbern(psi)
       s[i] ~ dcat(probs[1:nPix])
       x0g[i] <- Sgrid[s[i],1]            ## get the xy coordinates of the s[i] pixel
       y0g[i] <- Sgrid[s[i],2]
       for(j in 1:J) {
          dist[i,j] <- (x0g[i] - X[j,1])^2 + (y0g[i] - X[j,2])^2
          lam[i,j] <- lam0*exp(-dist[i,j]/(2*sigma^2))*z[i]
          y[i,j]~ dpois(lam[i,j]*K)
       }
    }
    N<- sum(z[1:M])
})

constants <- list(M=M,                 ## agumented individuals
                          K=K,                 ## effort
                          J=J,                  ## ntraps
                          Sgrid=Sgrid,      ## grid coordinates
                          nPix=nPix)        ## number of cells on grid

data <- list(y=y,                          ## capture history (ind x J)
                  X=X,                         ## trap coordinates
                  probs=probs)            ## prob of si be in each grid cell

## Initial values
initscoord <- X[sample(dim(X)[1],M,replace=TRUE),1:2]
sst <- rep(0,dim(initscoord)[1])
for(i in 1:length(sst)) {
    sst[i] <- which(apply(Sgrid,1,identical,initscoord[i,]))
}
z <- rep(1,M)

inits <- list (sigma=0.5, lam0=0.1, psi=0.5, s=sst, z=z)

Rmodel <- nimbleModel(code=code, constants=constants, data=data, inits=inits)

Thank you, and my apologies if this is a repeated posting.

Bruna Amaral

> Dear Yan,

>
> 1. You could translate them into nimbleFunctions.  Obviously that provides limited features but can work well for primarily numerical functions.
>

>
> 3. You could call them from nimbleFunctions an R calls, which are executed in R, even from compiled nimbleFunctions.  Often a wrapper will be needed to achieve clean types. messages.subject: Re: Translate R functions into Nimble
messages.subject_clean: Translate R functions into Nimble
messages.body_plain:
You can't use a formula as an object in compiled nimble code.  You would have to wrap your call to xtabs in another R function that you could call from a nimbleFunction and that would then call xtabs and provide the formula.  If the formula is always the same, doing it this way should be easy.  If it is one from a simple set of options, you could pass an integer argument to select the one you need, or use some similar kind of approach.
-Perry
